full_judgment:
A.M. Mahmudur Rahman J: This second appeal at the instance of defendant No. 3 is against the judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, First Court, Chittagong reversing those of the learned Munsif, First Court, Sadar, and Chittagong. 

 4. The trial court decreed the suit against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2 and dismissed against the defendant No. 3. Defendant Nos. 1 and 2 took an appeal against said decree. The lower appellate court, however, allowed the appeal and decreed the suit against defendant No. 3 the appellant with costs and dismissed the same against the defendant Nos. 1 and 2. Against that decree the defendant No. 3 filed this second appeal. 

 5. Mr. Fazlul Karim argues that for want of notice under section 109 of the Chittagong Port Act, 1914 the suit was barred against the defendant No. 3 the Trustee of the Port of Chittagong and the lower appellate court erred in law in decreeing the suit against the defendant No. 3, the appellant. He further contends that there being landing of un-manifested cargo it was the duty of the consignee to locate the same following nil mark procedure and the consignee not having been done so his client has no responsibility for the loss of goods in view of the provisions of sub-rules (f) and (g) of Rule 64 ofGeneral Rules and Schedules for Working of Chittagong Port (Railway) Jetties and the lower appellate court fell into an error of law in decreeingthe suit against the appellant 

 11. It appears from evidence Ext. D that 209 drums landed from the ship under nil wrong or obliterated mark, out of those 209 drums only 54 drums were available and 155 drums not available in the Jetty although the same landed from the ship without any mark. Mr. Karim submits that when the claim of the plaintiff was for the price of 13 drums and when the evidence shows that 54 drums were still available in the Jetty premises at the time of joint checking, the consignee ought to have followed the nil mark procedure for those drums and that not being done the Port Authority was immuned from any liability in view of the provision of Rule 64 (0 and (g). It is true that under section 50A of the Chittagong Port Act the Port Authority is responsible for the loss of goods landed and remained in its possession or control as a bailee in view of the provisions of sections 151,152 and 161 of the Contract Act, 1872. But section 50A will not operate in a case where the goods landed under nil mark and the consignee fails to follow the nil mark procedure to locate the goods by reason of sub-rules (f) and (g) of Rule 64 of General Rules and the Schedules for Working of the Chittagong Port (Railway) Jetties. In this case as the owner of the drums did not remove the same from the jetty premises, without any fault on the part of the Jetty administration, within clear 7 working days from the time of landing of the drums in question the Jetty Administration is not liable for any loss as in this case the Port Authority informed the owner of the drums to find out the same and there was no fault on the part of the Port Authority to locate the goods. This view also finds support from the following observation of the learned Judges of the Appellate Division The Port Authority did not inform the plaintiff nor make any serious effort to find as to what happened to the goods that had been delivered." 12. For the reasons stated above, I allow this appeal and set aside the judgment and decree of the lower appellate court and dismiss the suit against the defendants.
